      New plans emerge to revive Lincoln’s Cornhill Market amid 'warts and all' review

      It's been running at a loss - but experts think there's a way to make the heart of Lincoln's independent businesses

      Comments7
      What's On
      Jamie Waller Local Democracy Reporter
      15:23, 06 Oct 2026
      Listen to audio version of this article
      Sponsored by
      0:00 / 2:53
      Instaread

      Lincoln leaders will consider whether to outsource running of the Cornhill Market as they draw up a business plan to turn its fortunes around.

      ‌

      The authority has admitted that the city centre venue hasn’t met expectations since it opened two-and-a-half years ago, and has consistently run at a loss.

      ‌

      Market specialists Next Phase have carried out a “warts and all” review, and their recommendations for a new business plan will be discussed at next week’s Executive meeting.

      ‌

      The council will also consider whether it will continue to run the £8 million market itself or outsource some or all of the work.

      Cause of fire which closed Lincolnshire village school confirmed

      Police drug expert sacked for stealing Red Bull drinks and snacks from cannabis factory

      The new vision describes it as “a home for small businesses in the heart of the city, where fresh food, cooked food, interesting retailers, artisan makers, and specialists sit side by side”.

      It proposes a range of changes to attract more footfall and encourage customers to spend more time in the venue.

      ‌

      There would be weekly themed markets, community activities, monthly late-night openings, and music events.

      The business plan would be built around several priorities:

      • Increasing occupancy rates and reduce the ‘churn’ of stalls coming and leaving
      • Increasing daily footfall and the amount of time people spend in the market
      • Increasing the number of new businesses starting at the market
      • Narrowing the operating deficit and increasing event income to create a financially stable position
      • Tracking and improving customer satisfaction, trader confidence and non-visitor perception.
      ‌

      Council leaders will make a decision on whether to outsource direct management of the market at the Executive meeting on Tuesday, October 13.

      Next Phase says the market isn’t in crisis, but is struggling like many in the sector.

      The market currently has 69 per cent occupancy, up from a low of 38 per cent at one point last year.

      ‌

      Councillor Joshua Wells, the portfolio holder for economic growth, said experts are confident that the market can improve.

      “Their assessment found that while there was a strong vision for Cornhill Market, the way it has been run hasn’t always matched that vision,” he said.

      “The market was originally run using a more traditional approach, focused largely on renting stalls rather than operating as a modern commercial destination.

      Article continues below

      “At the same time, the operational structures and resources weren’t always aligned with the specialist skills needed to deliver that ambition.

      “Over time, this led to decisions which moved away from the original plan, which has affected trader and customer confidence.”

        1. Comment by LooksAskance.

          14 hrs ago

          People loved the old market for its butcher, fishmonger, greengrocer, florist etc. These were kept separate from the other stalls.

          Inside there were stalls selling useful goods such as haberdashery, school uniform, pet food, rucksacks and bags, knitting yarn, books and music etc.

          Now there are a lot of niche, and rather unnecessary items, surrounded by smelly fast food.

          For me personally, I don't like to buy any clothing or items which have been surrounded by kitchens for hours or days, as one can smell the fat, onions, garlic etc.

          I have the same problem with The Stack, which is a good venue and has some fun events, but one returns home, after an evening out there, smelling like a fast-food kitchen.

          The council - and their advisors - have not thought this through.

          The food outlets need to be enclosed, with good extraction and ventilation, and kept away from the other products.
